entries_new.name: British Antarctic Territory claim
entries_new.laws: Antarctic Treaty, in force 1961, freezes the claim
entries_new.challenge: Argentina and Chile claim overlapping areas
entries_new.recognition: Recognised by Australia, France, New Zealand and Norway, whose claims do not overlap with it
entries_new.mechanism: A colonial declaration, justified by whaling regulation, was later widened by rewording the sector out to the Pole.
entries_new.story: The United Kingdom claims a sector of Antarctica between 20 and 80 degrees west of Greenwich. In 1908 it declared sovereignty over South Georgia, the South Orkneys, the South Shetlands, the South Sandwich Islands and Graham's Land, south of 50 degrees south. It said it needed to regulate and tax the whaling industry. A 1917 rewording extended the claim to the South Pole. The area was run from the Falkland Islands until 1962, when it became a separate British Overseas Territory. Argentina and Chile claim overlapping ground.
entries_new.anchor: Sector from 20 to 80 degrees west, south of 60 degrees south

entries_new.name: Ross Dependency
entries_new.founder: United Kingdom, administered by New Zealand
entries_new.laws: Antarctic Treaty, in force 1961, freezes the claim
entries_new.recognition: Recognised by the United Kingdom, Australia, France and Norway
entries_new.mechanism: An imperial Order in Council named a governor for land nobody lived on.
entries_new.story: The Ross Dependency is New Zealand's claimed sector of Antarctica, between 160 degrees east and 150 degrees west, south of 60 degrees south. It began on 30 July 1923, when the British government issued an Order in Council under the British Settlements Act 1887 and named the Governor-General of New Zealand as its governor. Britain's Colonial Under-Secretary Leopold Amery had written that it was desirable for the whole of Antarctica to be included in the British Empire. Claims in the area have been frozen since the 1961 Antarctic Treaty.
entries_new.anchor: Sector from 160 degrees east to 150 degrees west, south of 60 degrees south

entries_new.name: Australian Antarctic Territory
entries_new.laws: Antarctic Treaty, in force 1961, freezes the claim
entries_new.recognition: Recognised by the United Kingdom, France, New Zealand and Norway
entries_new.mechanism: Britain handed over land that an Australian-led expedition had surveyed, using an imperial order.
entries_new.story: The Australian Antarctic Territory is the largest Antarctic claim, covering the sector south of 60 degrees south between 160 and 45 degrees east. A British imperial order transferred it to Australia in 1933. It followed the British Australian and New Zealand Antarctic Research Expedition of 1929 to 1931, led by the geologist Douglas Mawson, which the article says established the claim to 42 percent of Antarctica. Britain had claimed Enderby Land in 1930. The 1961 Antarctic Treaty froze the claim.
entries_new.anchor: Sector from 160 to 45 degrees east, south of 60 degrees south

entries_new.name: Adélie Land claim
entries_new.laws: Antarctic Treaty, in force 1961, freezes the claim
entries_new.recognition: Recognised by the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and Norway
entries_new.mechanism: A flag-raising and possession ceremony by a naval explorer, accepted decades later by Britain.
entries_new.story: France claims Adélie Land, a coastal strip of Antarctica. The claim rests on a landing by the explorer Jules Dumont d'Urville, who raised the French flag and took possession at 17:30 on 21 January 1840 and named the coast after his wife Adèle. Britain eventually recognised the claim, and the border with the Australian Antarctic Territory was fixed in 1938. France later built Dumont d'Urville Station and Charcot Station there. Claims in Antarctica have been frozen since the 1961 treaty.
entries_new.anchor: Coast south of 60 degrees south, near 140 degrees east

entries_new.name: Queen Maud Land claim
entries_new.laws: Royal decree of 14 January 1939; Antarctic Treaty freezes the claim
entries_new.challenge: Disputed in 1939 by the United States, Chile, the Soviet Union and Germany
entries_new.recognition: Recognised by the United Kingdom, Australia, France and New Zealand
entries_new.mechanism: A decree issued to protect whaling access, timed just before a rival expedition arrived.
entries_new.story: Norway claims Queen Maud Land, named for Queen Maud of Wales after a 1929 expedition. The whale-ship owner Lars Christensen paid for expeditions so that Norwegian whalers would avoid British taxation of whaling stations. Norway annexed the land by royal decree on 14 January 1939, five days before a German expedition arrived. The United States, Chile, the Soviet Union and Germany disputed the claim. A 1948 agreement with Britain set its limits at 20 degrees west to 45 degrees east.
entries_new.anchor: Sector from 20 degrees west to 45 degrees east

entries_new.name: New Swabia
entries_new.stopped_by: No formal claim was ever made; Norway had annexed Queen Maud Land five days earlier
entries_new.mechanism: Aerial mapping and dropped markers were meant to support a later claim that was never filed.
entries_new.story: New Swabia is the name given to part of Queen Maud Land photographed by a German expedition. The 1938 German Antarctic Expedition, led by Alfred Ritscher, reached the pack ice off Antarctica in the ship Schwabenland on 19 January 1939. It photographed about 350,000 square kilometres from the air and dropped darts marked with swastikas every 26 kilometres. Germany never made a formal claim or built a lasting base. The article says the claim was disputed at the time and is not taken into account today.
entries_new.anchor: Part of Queen Maud Land, roughly 0 degrees longitude

entries_new.name: Ecuador's Antarctic claim
entries_new.laws: Article 4 of the 2008 Constitution of Ecuador
entries_new.challenge: Overlaps the Chilean claim and Norway's island claim; the Antarctic Treaty bars claims after 1961
entries_new.mechanism: A national declaration, later written into a constitution, made after the treaty froze new claims.
entries_new.story: Ecuador declared in 1967 a right to an Antarctic area between 84 degrees 30 minutes and 95 degrees 30 minutes west. The claim was ratified in 1987 and is included in Article 4 of Ecuador's 2008 Constitution. It overlaps Chile's claim and Norway's claim to its Antarctic island. It came after the 1961 Antarctic Treaty, which says no activity after 1961 can be the basis of a territorial claim and that no new claim can be made.
entries_new.anchor: Sector from 84.5 to 95.5 degrees west

entries_new.name: Iran's 2013 statement on a South Pole sector
entries_new.challenge: Conflicts with Australia's claim; the Antarctic Treaty bars new claims
entries_new.mechanism: A latitude-based argument, of the kind used in the sector theory that older claimants rely on.
entries_new.story: In March 2013 Mohammad Bagheri, of Iran's General Staff of the Armed Forces, said that Iran can claim sovereignty over part of the South Pole under international law according to latitude. He pointed to access through the Makran Sea and to the lack of land between Iran's eastern coast and Antarctica. The sector described would be about 3,000 km long and 405 km wide, 200,000 to 250,000 square kilometres, and would conflict with Australia's claim and include Mawson Station. Wikipedia lists it under possible future claims.
entries_new.anchor: Sector described as overlapping the Australian claim near Mawson Station

entries_new.name: Operation Highjump and the US reservation of Antarctic claims
entries_new.recognition: None; the United States and Russia say they reserve the right to claim
entries_new.mechanism: A large military expedition with a stated scientific goal and, per the source, an aim of widening US sovereignty.
entries_new.story: The United States made no claim in Antarctica but kept the right to make one. Operation Highjump ran from 1946 to 1947 under Rear Admiral Richard Byrd with 4,700 men, 13 ships and aircraft, and built the base Little America IV. Wikipedia says the mission was also aimed at consolidating and extending United States sovereignty over the largest practicable area, although this was publicly denied before the expedition ended. The United States and the Soviet Union both filed reservations against the treaty's ban on new claims.
entries_new.anchor: Antarctica; the source gives no site for Little America IV

entries_new.name: Operation Tabarin
entries_new.stopped_by: Handed to a civilian survey body in 1945
entries_new.challenge: Argentina and, provoked by it, Chile
entries_new.mechanism: Bases, stamps and post offices were placed to show administration of the claimed land.
entries_new.story: Operation Tabarin was a British wartime expedition begun in 1943 to assert British claims and set up a permanent presence in Antarctica. The Foreign Office worried about United States postwar activity, and a cover story spoke of denying the area to German ships. Personnel removed Argentine flags from Deception Island. Bases followed at Deception Island, Port Lockroy and Hope Bay, with post offices, signposts, plaques and stamps as signs of sovereignty. In 1945 the bases passed to the Falkland Islands Dependencies Survey, later the British Antarctic Survey.
entries_new.anchor: Deception Island, Port Lockroy and Hope Bay area

entries_new.name: Argentine Antarctica
entries_new.laws: Decree 8944 of 2 September 1946; Antarctic Treaty freezes the claim
entries_new.challenge: Overlaps British and Chilean claims; Britain protested the South Orkneys base
entries_new.mechanism: Maps and decrees, backed by a purchased station and later bases, were used to set the sector limits.
entries_new.story: Argentina claims an Antarctic sector it calls Argentine Antarctica. It bought a meteorological station on Laurie Island from the Scottish expedition leader William Bruce for 5,000 pesos in 1904 and reported a permanent base in the South Orkneys in 1906, which Britain disputed. In January 1942 Argentina declared its rights between 25 and 68 degrees 34 minutes west, and Decree 8944 of 1946 extended the mapped sector to 74 degrees west. In 1952 Argentine troops fired a machine gun over British staff at Hope Bay and later apologised.
entries_new.anchor: Sector from 25 to 74 degrees west, south of 60 degrees south

entries_new.name: Chilean Antarctic Territory
entries_new.laws: Decree 1747 of 1940; Antarctic Treaty freezes the claim
entries_new.challenge: Argentina protested in 1940; the claim overlaps British and Argentine areas
entries_new.mechanism: An inherited-borders argument based on a Spanish colonial grant.
entries_new.story: Chile claims a sector of Antarctica, set by Decree 1747 of 6 November 1940 under President Pedro Aguirre Cerda. The decree rests on uti possidetis juris, the idea that a new state keeps the borders of the earlier colonial unit. Chile points to a 1539 Spanish grant of the lands south of the Strait of Magellan and to a Spanish governorate transferred to Chile in 1555. Argentina protested on 12 November 1940. The claim overlaps Argentine and British claims, and the 1961 Antarctic Treaty freezes it.
entries_new.anchor: Sector south of 60 degrees south, with 53 degrees west as the eastern edge

entries_new.name: Governorate of Terra Australis, the Spanish basis for Chilean and Argentine claims
entries_new.challenge: Other claimants do not accept the argument
entries_new.mechanism: Inherited title from a colonial-era royal grant, cited as proof that Spain intended to occupy.
entries_new.story: Argentina and Chile both argue that Spain held rights in Antarctica. In 1539 King Charles V granted Pedro Sánchez de la Hoz a governorship covering all lands south of the Strait of Magellan, which they read to include Antarctica. De la Hoz transferred the title to Pedro de Valdivia in 1540, and in 1555 the claim was incorporated into Chile. The two countries also cite the 1493 papal bull Inter caetera and the 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas. Modern Spain has made no Antarctic claim.
entries_new.anchor: Strait of Magellan region, southern tip of South America

entries_new.name: Brazil, Peru and Uruguay and their reserved Antarctic rights
entries_new.challenge: The Antarctic Treaty bars new claims
entries_new.mechanism: Reservation statements and a proposed meridian-based theory instead of a formal claim.
entries_new.story: Three South American states have kept open the possibility of an Antarctic claim without making one. Wikipedia reports speculation that Brazil might claim a sector between 53 and 28 degrees west, which would overlap Argentina and Britain but not Chile, and says Brazil proposes a meridian theory that would give it and others a claim. Peru reserved its rights under the principle of Antarctic defrontation, citing climate, ecology, geology and history. Uruguay joined the Antarctic Treaty System with a declaration reserving its rights.
entries_new.anchor: South Atlantic sector, 28 to 53 degrees west (speculative)

entries_new.name: LIFE Pathfinder (Sierra Space)
entries_new.mechanism: A privately built station still needs launch licences and authorisation from the builder's home state under the Outer Space Treaty.
entries_new.story: LIFE Pathfinder is a proposed free-flying test version of LIFE, the inflatable space habitat of the American company Sierra Space. An inflatable habitat launches folded and expands in orbit. Wikipedia lists it at 285 cubic metres of pressurised volume with a 2026 target, and quotes SpaceNews from June 2023 saying Sierra Space proposed to fly it as soon as the end of 2026, before offering LIFE for Orbital Reef. The listing is private and gives no crew size. It would operate under US licensing, not as territory of its own.

entries_new.mechanism: A privately built module, planned to fly under launch and operating licences from the United States.
entries_new.story: StarMax is a proposed single-module space station from the American company Gravitics. The company describes it as providing up to 400 cubic metres of habitable volume, which it says is nearly half the volume of the International Space Station in one module. Wikipedia's list of planned stations gives a 2026 target, a private programme and no crew size. entries_new.story: Thunderbird Station is a space station proposed by the American company Max Space. On 17 December 2025 Max Space said that, because NASA had revised its Commercial LEO Destinations programme, it was proposing a single-launch station built on its inflatable habitat technology. The station would expand to 350 cubic metres in orbit, support four people, and use two docking ports for resupply and crew rotation. Wikipedia lists a 2029 launch date. Max Space is a private company and its figures are its own plans.

entries_new.stopped_by: Lack of funds; the company went defunct in 2016
entries_new.mechanism: Buying surplus Soviet station hardware and registering the company in a small jurisdiction, with a launch never achieved.
entries_new.story: Excalibur Almaz was a private spaceflight company headquartered in Douglas, on the Isle of Man, founded in 2005 and defunct by 2016. It acquired Soviet-era Almaz hardware, which was originally a military station programme, and planned crew and cargo flights, with lunar and deep space services added in January 2012. In October 2011 it signed an unfunded Space Act Agreement with NASA. Wikipedia lists its commercial Almaz station as cancelled in 2016 for lack of funds, with the hardware never launched.

entries_new.story: In July 2024 the Japanese space agency JAXA announced that it had contracted the trading company Mitsui & Co. to develop a concept for a new space station module. The module would eventually fly to and dock with an American private space station that had not yet been chosen at the time of the announcement. entries_new.name: Outer Space Treaty of 1967
entries_new.founder: United Nations negotiators; United States, United Kingdom and Soviet Union as first signatories
entries_new.laws: Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space, including the Moon and Other Celestial Bodies
entries_new.challenge: Private claimants such as lunar deed sellers read it as silent on individuals
entries_new.mechanism: States agree not to claim sovereignty over celestial bodies, and each state answers for its private citizens' space activities.
entries_new.story: The Outer Space Treaty is the base treaty of space law. It opened for signature in the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union on 27 January 1967 and entered into force on 10 October 1967. By October 2025 it had 118 parties. Article 2 says outer space, including the Moon, is not subject to national appropriation by claim of sovereignty, use, occupation or any other means. Article 6 makes states responsible for private space activities. Sellers of Moon plots argue that it binds only nations.
entries_new.anchor: United States, centre of the country; the treaty opened for signature in the United States, the United Kingdom and the Soviet Union
entries_new.cov_type: Lunar deed sellers and space nations

entries_new.name: Space Liability Convention of 1972
entries_new.laws: Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, 1972
entries_new.mechanism: The launching state carries liability, which ties every private launch to a state that can be held to account.
entries_new.story: The Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects expands the liability rules of the Outer Space Treaty. It opened for signature on 29 March 1972 and entered into force on 1 September 1972. A state is fully liable for damage from any space object launched from its territory or facility, or whose launch it caused. Two launching states are jointly liable. Only states can bring claims. The only claim filed under it followed the 1978 crash of the Soviet satellite Kosmos 954 in Canada.
entries_new.anchor: United Nations treaty, no fixed place; pinned at the centre of the United States
entries_new.cov_type: Lunar deed sellers and space nations

entries_new.name: Space Registration Convention of 1975
entries_new.laws: Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space
entries_new.mechanism: Each launching state reports its space objects to the United Nations register.
entries_new.story: The Convention on Registration of Objects Launched into Outer Space was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1974 and went into force in 1976. Launching states must give the United Nations details of each space object: the launching state, a designator or registration number, the date and place of launch, basic orbit data and the general function. The register is kept by the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs. As of January 2026, 78 states had ratified it.
entries_new.anchor: United Nations treaty, no fixed place; pinned at the centre of the United States
entries_new.cov_type: Lunar deed sellers and space nations

entries_new.name: Rescue Agreement of 1968
entries_new.laws: Agreement on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space
entries_new.mechanism: Duties of rescue and return follow the launching state's ownership of the craft, not any claim to the land where it comes down.
entries_new.story: The Agreement on the Rescue of Astronauts, the Return of Astronauts and the Return of Objects Launched into Outer Space was adopted on 19 December 1967 and entered into force on 3 December 1968. A state that learns spacecraft personnel are in distress must notify the launching authority and the UN Secretary-General, and must help rescue personnel who land in its territory. Where distress occurs beyond any nation's territory, states able to help must assist. As of January 2022, 98 states had ratified it.
entries_new.anchor: United Nations treaty, no fixed place; pinned at the centre of the United States
entries_new.cov_type: Lunar deed sellers and space nations

entries_new.name: Magna Carta of Space (William Hyman, 1966)
entries_new.stopped_by: Superseded by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty
entries_new.mechanism: A legal argument that space is held in common, so no one can take it by occupation.
entries_new.story: The Magna Carta of Space was a 1966 proposal by William A. Hyman. According to Wikipedia it framed outer space explicitly as res communis, a thing held in common, and not as terra nullius, land that belongs to nobody and can be taken. Wikipedia says the framing later influenced the work of the United Nations Committee on the Peaceful Uses of Outer Space. The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 then set out space as the province of all mankind and barred national appropriation.
entries_new.anchor: United States, centre of the country; the sources read do not give Hyman's base

entries_new.name: Richard Garriott's purchase of Lunokhod 2
entries_new.mechanism: Buying a spacecraft that already sits on the Moon, then joking that the ground around it belongs to the buyer.
entries_new.story: In 1993 Richard Garriott, the creator of the Ultima computer games, bought the Lunokhod 2 rover and its Luna 21 lander from the Russian Lavochkin bureau, which had been part of the Soviet space programme. Wikipedia calls it the first private purchase of an object on another astronomical body. Described as not bound by international agreements, he jokingly claimed the rest of the Moon in the name of his game character Lord British, or at least the area around the two objects and the 39 km path the rover drove.

entries_new.name: Peter I Island, a Norwegian dependency
entries_new.founder: Norway, via Lars Christensen's Norvegia expedition
entries_new.pop: Uninhabited; an automatic weather station since 1987
entries_new.laws: Royal proclamation of 6 March 1931; Antarctic Treaty since 1961
entries_new.recognition: Recognised by the United Kingdom, Australia, France and New Zealand
entries_new.mechanism: A landing, a flag-claim and a royal proclamation, motivated by avoiding British whaling taxes.
entries_new.story: This uninhabited volcanic island lies in the Bellingshausen Sea, 450 kilometres from continental Antarctica, claimed by Norway. It is 11 by 19 kilometres and nearly covered by a glacier. Nobody set foot on it until 2 February 1929, when the Norvegia expedition of Nils Larsen and Ola Olstad, financed by the whale-ship owner Lars Christensen, landed and claimed it. A royal proclamation placed it under Norwegian sovereignty on 6 March 1931, and it became a dependency on 23 March 1933. It has been under the Antarctic Treaty since 1961.
entries_new.anchor: Peter I Island, Bellingshausen Sea

entries_new.name: Lithuania's data embassy in Luxembourg
entries_new.laws: Bilateral headquarters agreement, modelled on diplomatic law, awaiting ratification at the time of the article
entries_new.recognition: An agreement between two recognised states
entries_new.mechanism: Servers in a friendly country get diplomatic-style immunity, so the state's records survive loss of its own territory.
entries_new.story: Lithuania and Luxembourg signed a headquarters agreement on 12 October, the year not given in the article read, for a Lithuanian data embassy in Luxembourg. The foreign ministers Xavier Bettel and Kęstutis Budrys signed it. Lithuania would protect some public data and critical systems there, with the most sensitive data staying in Lithuanian data centres and copies held remotely so digital services can restart. The article said the agreement still needed ratification by the Luxembourg Chamber of Deputies and that the site does not become Lithuanian territory.
entries_new.anchor: Luxembourg; the data centre site is not named

sources.t: Lithuania is to set up its data embassy in Luxembourg, Paperjam

entries_new.name: Bahrain's 2018 Cloud Law
entries_new.laws: Legislative decree of 2018 (Cloud Law)
entries_new.mechanism: A host state lets foreign customers' data follow the customer's home law inside its data centres.
entries_new.story: In 2018 Bahrain issued a legislative decree, known as the Cloud Law, creating a legal framework for data stored in Bahraini data centres. Data held there is subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the customer's domestic law, not Bahrain's. Wikipedia's article on data embassies lists it with the Estonian arrangement in Luxembourg. A Google Cloud article cites it as a host framework and names no country that has set up a data embassy under it.
entries_new.anchor: Bahrain, approximate centre

sources.t: Data embassies: strengthening resiliency with sovereignty, Google Cloud
